title: “All nations shall flow unto it” (Isaiah) — “people shall flow unto it” (Micah): the same vision with “nations” and “people” exchanged
summary: Isaiah 2 and Micah 4 give almost the same vision of the mountain of the Lord. In the KJV, Isaiah says all nations flow to the mountain and many people go up, while Micah says people flow to it and many nations come; Isaiah’s Lord rebukes many people, while Micah’s rebukes strong nations afar off. The Hebrew words are not the same in the two books at these points.
text: KJV Isaiah 2:2: “and all nations shall flow unto it.” KJV Micah 4:1: “and people shall flow unto it.” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 2:2: וְהָיָ֣ה ׀ בְּאַחֲרִ֣ית הַיָּמִ֗ים נָכֹ֨ון יִֽהְיֶ֜ה הַ֤ר בֵּית־יְהוָה֙ בְּרֹ֣אשׁ הֶהָרִ֔ים וְנִשָּׂ֖א מִגְּבָעֹ֑ות וְנָהֲר֥וּ אֵלָ֖יו כָּל־הַגֹּויִֽם׃. Hebrew (WLC) Micah 4:1: וְהָיָ֣ה ׀ בְּאַחֲרִ֣ית הַיָּמִ֗ים יִ֠הְיֶה הַ֣ר בֵּית־יְהוָ֤ה נָכֹון֙ בְּרֹ֣אשׁ הֶהָרִ֔ים וְנִשָּׂ֥א ה֖וּא מִגְּבָעֹ֑ות וְנָהֲר֥וּ עָלָ֖יו עַמִּֽים ׃. KJV Isaiah 2:3: “And many people shall go and say, Come ye, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord.” KJV Micah 4:2: “And many nations shall come, and say, Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord.” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 2:3: וְֽהָלְכ֞וּ עַמִּ֣ים רַבִּ֗ים וְאָמְרוּ֙ לְכ֣וּ ׀ וְנַעֲלֶ֣ה אֶל־הַר־יְהוָ֗ה אֶל־בֵּית֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְיֹרֵ֙נוּ֙ מִדְּרָכָ֔יו וְנֵלְכָ֖ה בְּאֹרְחֹתָ֑יו כִּ֤י מִצִּיֹּון֙ תֵּצֵ֣א תֹורָ֔ה וּדְבַר־יְהוָ֖ה מִירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃. Hebrew (WLC) Micah 4:2: וְֽהָלְכ֞וּ גֹּויִ֣ם רַבִּ֗ים וְאָֽמְרוּ֙ לְכ֣וּ ׀ וְנַעֲלֶ֣ה אֶל־הַר־יְהוָ֗ה וְאֶל־בֵּית֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְיֹורֵ֙נוּ֙ מִדְּרָכָ֔יו וְנֵלְכָ֖ה בְּאֹֽרְחֹתָ֑יו כִּ֤י מִצִּיֹּון֙ תֵּצֵ֣א  תֹורָ֔ה וּדְבַר־יְהוָ֖ה מִירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃. KJV Isaiah 2:4: “and shall rebuke many people”. KJV Micah 4:3: “and rebuke strong nations afar off”. Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 2:4: וְשָׁפַט֙ בֵּ֣ין הַגֹּויִ֔ם וְהֹוכִ֖יחַ לְעַמִּ֣ים רַבִּ֑ים וְכִתְּת֨וּ חַרְבֹותָ֜ם לְאִתִּ֗ים וַחֲנִיתֹֽותֵיהֶם֙ לְמַזְמֵרֹ֔ות לֹא־יִשָּׂ֨א גֹ֤וי אֶל־גֹּוי֙ חֶ֔רֶב וְלֹא־יִלְמְד֥וּ עֹ֖וד מִלְחָמָֽה׃  פ. Hebrew (WLC) Micah 4:3: וְשָׁפַ֗ט בֵּ֚ין עַמִּ֣ים רַבִּ֔ים וְהֹוכִ֛יחַ לְגֹויִ֥ם עֲצֻמִ֖ים עַד־רָחֹ֑וק וְכִתְּת֨וּ חַרְבֹתֵיהֶ֜ם לְאִתִּ֗ים וַחֲנִיתֹֽתֵיהֶם֙ לְמַזְמֵרֹ֔ות לֹֽא־יִשְׂא֞וּ גֹּ֤וי אֶל־גֹּוי֙ חֶ֔רֶב וְלֹא־יִלְמְד֥וּן עֹ֖וד מִלְחָמָֽה׃. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/2/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/33/4/.
reasoning: The two passages run in the same order and share most of their wording, but the nouns for the peoples differ. Isaiah has all the nations (כָּל־הַגּוֹיִם) flowing and many peoples (עַמִּים רַבִּים) saying “Come”; Micah has peoples (עַמִּים) flowing and many nations (גּוֹיִם רַבִּים) saying “Come”. In Isaiah the Lord rebukes many peoples (לְעַמִּים רַבִּים); in Micah he rebukes strong nations afar off (לְגוֹיִם עֲצֻמִּים עַד־רָחוֹק). Whichever book is read, the same two words appear, in swapped places. Micah 4:4 also adds the vine and fig tree and the Lord’s mouth having spoken, which Isaiah 2 does not have.
scope: This is a direct wording contrast between two passages, KJV against KJV, shown with the Hebrew beside it. It is untagged: no translation difference is claimed, because the KJV renders each Hebrew word by its usual English word. The record does not say which book quotes the other, whether both draw on a third source, or that the nations/peoples distinction carries a different doctrine; in Hebrew poetry גּוֹיִם and עַמִּים often stand in parallel and may mean much the same. The record also does not treat Micah’s extra verse 4 as a conflict. The Joel 3:10 record is a separate comparison with the same swords and plowshares wording. title: “The seed of an homer shall yield an ephah” — the Greek says six artabas of seed make three measures
summary: The KJV describes a failed harvest: ten acres of vineyard give one bath, and a homer of seed gives an ephah. The Hebrew gives the same relation. Brenton’s Greek names different measures: ten yoke of oxen make one jar, and one who sows six artabas makes three measures.

Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 5:10: Οὗ γὰρ ἐργῶνται δέκα ζεύγη βοῶν, ποιήσει κεράμιον ἕν· καὶ ὁ σπείρων ἀρτάβας ἓξ, ποιήσει μέτρα τρία.. [where ten yoke of oxen plough, it will make one jar; and the one sowing six artabas will make three measures] Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ISA05.htm.
reasoning: In the Hebrew a homer of seed yields an ephah, and the KJV says so. In the Greek the sower sows six artabas and gets three measures, and the vineyard is measured by yoke (ζεύγη) of oxen, not acres, and the yield is a κεράμιον, a jar, not a bath. The units and the numbers differ: homer to ephah, and six to three.

The Greek names are taken from the page as printed; the record does not convert artabas, measures, baths, ephahs or homers into one another, and does not say what ratio each Greek measure expresses. title: “Even all the chief ones of the earth” — the Greek calls them “all the giants who ruled the earth”

title: “The brook of the willows” and “lions upon him that escapeth of Moab” — the Greek has the Lord bring Arabs

title: “As a forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch” — the Greek says “as the Amorites and the Hivites left”
summary: The KJV compares the strong cities to a forsaken bough and an uppermost branch. Brenton’s Greek compares them to what the Amorites and the Hivites left before the sons of Israel.
text: KJV Isaiah 17:9: “In that day shall his strong cities be as a forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch, which they left because of the children of Israel: and there shall be desolation.” Hebrew (WLC) 17:9: בַּיֹּ֨ום הַה֜וּא יִהְי֣וּ ׀ עָרֵ֣י מָעֻזֹּ֗ו כַּעֲזוּבַ֤ת הַחֹ֙רֶשׁ֙ וְהָ֣אָמִ֔יר אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָזְב֔וּ מִפְּנֵ֖י בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְהָיְתָ֖ה שְׁמָמָֽה׃. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 17:9: Τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ ἔσονται αἱ πόλεις σου ἐγκαταλελειμμέναι, ὃν τρόπον κατέλιπον οἱ Ἀμοῤῥαῖοι καὶ οἱ Εὐαῖοι ἀπὸ προσώπου τῶν νἱῶν Ἰσραήλ· καὶ ἔσονται ἔρημοι,. [as the Amorites and the Hivites left, because of the sons of Israel] Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/17/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ISA17.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew has כַּעֲזוּבַת הַחֹרֶשׁ וְהָאָמִיר, “like the forsaking of the חֹרֶשׁ and the אָמִיר”, which the KJV renders “a forsaken bough and an uppermost branch”. The Greek has ὃν τρόπον κατέλιπον οἱ Ἀμοῤῥαῖοι καὶ οἱ Εὐαῖοι, “as the Amorites and the Hivites left”. The Greek names two peoples where the KJV names two parts of a tree. Both end with “because of the children of Israel” and a desolation.

title: “Pul, and Lud, that draw the bow” — the Greek has a proper name, Mosoch, where the Hebrew has the words for drawing the bow
summary: The KJV has the survivors sent to Tarshish, Pul and Lud, “that draw the bow”, Tubal and Javan. Brenton’s Greek has Tharsis, Phoud, Loud and Mosoch (a proper name), Thobel and Hellas; “that draw the bow” is not in the Greek.
text: KJV Isaiah 66:19: “And I will set a sign among them, and I will send those that escape of them unto the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, that draw the bow, to Tubal, and Javan, to the isles afar off, that have not heard my fame, neither have seen my glory; and they shall declare my glory among the Gentiles.” Hebrew (WLC) 66:19: וְשַׂמְתִּ֨י בָהֶ֜ם אֹ֗ות וְשִׁלַּחְתִּ֣י מֵהֶ֣ם ׀ פְּ֠לֵיטִים אֶֽל־הַגֹּויִ֞ם תַּרְשִׁ֨ישׁ פּ֥וּל וְל֛וּד מֹ֥שְׁכֵי קֶ֖שֶׁת תֻּבַ֣ל וְיָוָ֑ן הָאִיִּ֣ים הָרְחֹקִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹא־שָׁמְע֤וּ אֶת־שִׁמְעִי֙ וְלֹא־רָא֣וּ אֶת־כְּבֹודִ֔י וְהִגִּ֥ידוּ אֶת־כְּבֹודִ֖י בַּגֹּויִֽם׃. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 66:19: Καὶ καταλείψω ἐπʼ αὐτῶν σημεῖον, καὶ ἐξαποστελῶ ἐξ αὐτῶν σεσωσμένους εἰς τὰ ἔθνη, εἰς Θαρσὶς, καὶ Φοὺδ, καὶ Λοὺδ, καὶ Μοσόχ, καὶ εἰς Θοβὲλ, καὶ εἰς τὴν Ἑλλάδα, καὶ εἰς τὰς νήσους τὰς πόῤῥω, οἳ οὐκ ἀκηκόασί μου τὸ ὄνομα, οὔτε ἑωράκασί μου τὴν δόξαν· καὶ ἀναγγελοῦσι τὴν δόξαν μου ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσι,. […to Tharsis, and Phoud, and Loud, and Mosoch, and to Thobel, and to Hellas, and to the far islands…] Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/66/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ISA66.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew has וְלוּד מֹשְׁכֵי קֶשֶׁת, “and Lud, drawers of the bow”, where מֹשְׁכֵי is a plural participle, “those drawing”. The Greek has καὶ Λοὺδ, καὶ Μοσόχ, “and Lud, and Mosoch”, and no word for bow. The KJV has a description of the people of Lud; the Greek has a separate place or people. Mosoch has the same consonants as the Hebrew name Meshech (מֶשֶׁךְ), which is not in this verse. Under the owner’s ruling on ordinary-word names this is the reverse case: the Greek has a name where the Hebrew has ordinary words.
scope: T applies at Isaiah 66:19 and only to “that draw the bow” against the name Mosoch. The record does not say the Hebrew should be read as Meshech, does not say the Greek translator read a different Hebrew text, and does not decide who is meant by Pul, Lud, Tubal or Javan; Javan/Hellas and Tarshish/Tharsis are usual equivalents and are not claimed as differences. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original, and the record does not claim the Greek is a mistranslation of the Hebrew. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

title: “Him that waiteth for him” (Isaiah) — “them that love him” (1 Corinthians): the quoted line is not worded the same
summary: 1 Corinthians 2:9 introduces its words with “as it is written” and says eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither entered into the heart of man the things God hath prepared for them that love him. The nearest verse in the KJV, Isaiah 64:4, says men have not heard nor perceived by the ear, neither hath the eye seen, O God, beside thee, what he hath prepared for him that waiteth for him. The wording differs in the persons, the order and the content.
text: KJV Isaiah 64:4: “For since the beginning of the world men have not heard, nor perceived by the ear, neither hath the eye seen, O God, beside thee, what he hath prepared for him that waiteth for him.” Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 64:3 (KJV 64:4): וּמֵעֹולָ֥ם לֹא־שָׁמְע֖וּ לֹ֣א הֶאֱזִ֑ינוּ עַ֣יִן לֹֽא־רָאָ֗תָה אֱלֹהִים֙ זוּלָ֣תְךָ֔ יַעֲשֶׂ֖ה לִמְחַכֵּה־לֹֽו׃. KJV 1 Corinthians 2:9: “But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.” Greek New Testament (SBLGNT) 1 Corinthians 2:9: ἀλλὰ καθὼς γέγραπται· Ἃ ὀφθαλμὸς οὐκ εἶδεν καὶ οὖς οὐκ ἤκουσεν καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἀνέβη, ὅσα ἡτοίμασεν ὁ θεὸς τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν αὐτόν.. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/64/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/SBLGNT/46/2/.
reasoning: Isaiah’s verse is addressed to God: the eye has not seen “a god beside you” who acts for the one who waits (לִמְחַכֵּה־לוֹ). Paul’s sentence is about what God prepared for those who love him (τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν αὐτόν). The two differ in the object (him that waiteth against them that love), in the order (ear then eye against eye then ear), and in the clause “neither have entered into the heart of man”, which the KJV Isaiah 64:4 does not have. The Hebrew has no verb for “entered into the heart”.
scope: This is a direct wording contrast between a passage and a later quotation of it, KJV against KJV, with the Hebrew and the Greek New Testament beside it. It is untagged: the record does not claim a mistranslation. It does not say Paul quotes Isaiah 64:4 alone; other passages (such as Isaiah 65:17) have been proposed as sources and the record does not decide between them. It does not say the New Testament author misquotes, since the introductory phrase “as it is written” does not say the quotation is word for word. The Septuagint of this verse (Brenton Isaiah 64:3 in his numbering) is a third wording and is not part of this record. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text; its verse numbers for Isaiah 64 run one lower than the KJV’s. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew and Greek manuscripts were not examined.
